subject: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
overview: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was a watchmaker's son from Geneva who, with almost no formal schooling, became one of the most disruptive writers of 18th-century Europe. Working mostly in France, he argued that civilization corrupts people who are naturally good, that political power is legitimate only when it rests on the will of the people, and that children should learn from experience rather than rote. His books were banned and burned in his lifetime, then adopted as gospel by the French revolutionaries a decade after his death.

key_moments.title: A revelation on the road to Vincennes
key_moments.text: Walking to visit his friend **Denis Diderot**, who was imprisoned at the Château de Vincennes, Rousseau read a prize question from the **Academy of Dijon** asking whether progress in the arts and sciences had improved morals. He answered no, arguing that refinement had made people more vain and less virtuous, and his **Discourse on the Arts and Sciences** won the prize in 1750, turning an obscure music copyist into a celebrity overnight. Rousseau later described the moment on the road as a sudden illumination so overwhelming that he sat down under a tree and found his shirt wet with tears.
claims: Denis Diderot was imprisoned at the Château de Vincennes in 1749.

key_moments.title: The Social Contract and Emile, then exile
key_moments.text: Within a few months Rousseau published **The Social Contract**, which opens with the line that man is born free and everywhere is in chains, and **Emile, or On Education**, a treatise on raising a child by nature rather than by books. Emile contained a section on religion, the Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar, that offended both Catholic and Protestant authorities: the **Parlement of Paris** condemned the book and ordered his arrest, and **Geneva**, the city he proudly signed himself a citizen of, burned both works. Rousseau spent the following years as a fugitive, moving between Swiss territories, including Môtiers in Prussian-ruled Neuchâtel, where locals reportedly stoned his house in 1765.

key_moments.title: Refuge in England and the quarrel with Hume
key_moments.text: The Scottish philosopher **David Hume** brought Rousseau to England in 1766 and helped arrange a pension from **King George III**. Rousseau settled at Wootton in Staffordshire, but he grew convinced that Hume was part of a plot to humiliate him, partly because of a mocking fake letter from the King of Prussia written by Horace Walpole that circulated in Paris. The falling-out became a public scandal when Hume published his side of the correspondence, and Rousseau returned to France in 1767: the two most famous thinkers of the age, briefly friends, ended as enemies in print.

key_moments.title: Death at Ermenonville and the Panthéon
key_moments.text: Rousseau died in 1778 at **Ermenonville**, north of Paris, on the estate of the Marquis de Girardin, and was buried on the Isle of Poplars in the park's lake, which became a site of pilgrimage. During the **French Revolution**, leaders such as **Maximilien Robespierre** treated his ideas of popular sovereignty and the general will as a founding creed, and in 1794 his remains were moved to the **Panthéon** in Paris. There he lies near **Voltaire**, the rival who mocked him for years and who had died in the same year, 1778.

deep_facts.text: The author of the most influential book on child-rearing of his century gave away every one of his own children. Rousseau and his companion Thérèse Levasseur had five children, and each was left at the Paris foundling hospital, where infant mortality was very high. The secret became public in 1764, when Voltaire published an anonymous pamphlet, The Sentiment of the Citizens, exposing it. Rousseau later confessed it himself in his Confessions, offering a series of justifications, and the contrast with Emile has haunted his reputation ever since.

deep_facts.text: Before he was a philosopher, Rousseau wanted to be a composer. In 1742 he presented the Paris Academy of Sciences with a new system of musical notation using numbers instead of notes on a staff; the Academy was unimpressed. A decade later his one-act opera Le Devin du village was performed before Louis XV at Fontainebleau in 1752 and was a hit, and the king's courtiers reported he hummed its tunes. Rousseau was invited to be presented to the king the next day, which would likely have brought a royal pension, and he chose not to go. For much of his life he earned his living as a copyist of music.

deep_facts.text: After the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, Voltaire wrote a poem attacking the idea that a benevolent Providence orders the world. Rousseau replied in a 1756 letter with an argument that sounds strikingly modern: nature had not built twenty thousand houses of six or seven storeys crowded together in Lisbon, and if the city's inhabitants had been spread out and housed more modestly, the damage would have been far smaller. Some scholars of disaster studies have pointed to the letter as an early claim that disasters are shaped as much by human choices as by nature.
claims: Voltaire wrote a poem on the 1755 Lisbon earthquake questioning divine Providence.

connections.name: Voltaire
connections.connection: His chief rival, who exposed the abandonment of his children in 1764 and now lies near him in the Panthéon.

connections.name: Denis Diderot
connections.connection: Close friend whose imprisonment at Vincennes in 1749 occasioned Rousseau's first discourse, before the two fell out in 1757.

connections.name: David Hume
connections.connection: Brought him to England in 1766, then became his public enemy after a bitter quarrel.

connections.name: French Revolution
connections.connection: Revolutionaries drew on his idea of the general will and moved his remains to the Panthéon in 1794.

connections.name: Maximilien Robespierre
connections.connection: An avowed admirer who invoked Rousseau's ideas of virtue and the general will during the Revolution.

connections.name: Encyclopédie
